[
1
]

The one thing that both Robert Tock and Evelyn Buchbinder Tock agree on
is that this is a tragic case.  They are both caring parents with three
wonderful children.  Unfortunately, these children have been caught in the
middle of their parents’ two and a half year battle.

[
2
]

This is an
action under the
Divorce Act
, R.S.C. 1985 c.3 (2nd Supp.).  While there
are support and property matters in dispute, the bulk of the trial involved the
care of the three children.

Background

[
3
]

Robert
Tock and Evelyn Buchbinder Tock were married on July 6, 1986.  They have three
children: Justin (17 years old), Goldie (14 years old) and Nili (7 years old).
They separated on July 3, 2003, but both continued to live in the matrimonial
home until Mr. Tock left on September 18, 2003.  At the current time, Nili’s
primary residence is with her mother, Justin’s primary residence is with his
father, and Goldie spends alternating weeks with each of her parents.

A. The Children

The Parties’ Positions

[
4
]

The key
issue between the parties is whether Goldie should continue to alternate her
residence between her parents’ homes or should live with her mother on a
full-time basis.  Other issues include whether the parents should co-parent the
three children and whether there should be any limitations placed on the
children’s exposure to their paternal grandmother, Mrs. Doris Tock.

[
5
]

Central to
Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s position that Goldie’s primary residence should be with
her is her assertion that Mr. Tock and his family have alienated the two older
children from her.  Mr. Tock denies that this has happened.   He maintains that
Goldie’s current living situation is working well and should continue for the
time being.  While Mr. Tock agrees that Goldie should eventually reside
primarily with her mother, it is his position that this should only happen when
Goldie wants it to happen.

[
6
]

The
parties also disagree on some ancillary matters: the allocation of holidays;
the timing of Mr. Tock’s visits with Nili; and the terms of future counselling.

Overarching Legal Principles

[
7
]

Section
16(8)
of the
Divorce Act

states that in making a custody order, the
court can only consider the best interests of the child as determined by
reference to the child’s conditions, means, needs and other circumstances.

[
8
]

Given Ms.
Buchbinder Tock’s allegation that parental alienation has occurred, section
16(10) is particularly relevant. It provides that the court must give effect to
the principle that a child should have as much contact with each parent as is
consistent with that child’s best interests and that the court should take into
consideration the willingness of the parent seeking custody to facilitate such
contact.

The Evidence

[
9
]

There was
considerable evidence during the trial about the conduct of Mr. Tock and Ms.
Buchbinder Tock, particularly during the period since separation.  Both accused
the other of escalating the dispute and behaving inappropriately.  However, s.
16(9) of the
Divorce Act
provides that past conduct is only relevant if
it speaks to the ability of the person to act as a parent. While I will address
the conduct of both parents, I will limit myself to highlighting the evidence
that is relevant to a determination of the children’s best interests.

Pre-Separation

[
10
]

Mr. Tock and Ms. Buchbinder Tock
agree that they have different parenting styles.  Rabbi Jossi Sapirman, who knew
the family very well prior to the separation, described Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s
approach as one of “good governance” while Mr. Tock’s approach was to be a
“pal”.  Dr. Goldstein described Ms. Buchbinder-Tock’s approach as more
authoritarian while Mr. Tock allowed the children more latitude and room for
deliberation and negotiation.

[
11
]

Their differing approaches to
parenting did not create a problem until Justin was 13 years old and in grade
7.  He started to have difficulties in school and to resist his parents’
authority.  Justin was grounded for several weekends when he failed to complete
his weekly homework assignments.  On a couple of occasions, he ran away to the
home of his cousin, David Tock.  In the spring of 2002, Justin called the
police, alleging that his father had assaulted him.

[
12
]

To address Justin’s difficulties,
the parents sought counselling and moved Justin to a more academically
challenging school in September 2002.  Whether it was the change of school or
for other reasons, Justin’s problems appear to have reduced significantly. Ms.
Buchbinder Tock reported that once he started at the new school, he was a
different person; he was happy again and did well both socially and
academically.  She testified that, immediately prior to the end of September
2003, she and Justin were getting much closer.

[
13
]

Mr. Tock’s mother, Doris Tock, and
his sister, Esther Tock, have a different version of Justin’s situation.  They
both testified that prior to the separation, Justin was unhappy.  They felt
that Ms. Buchbinder Tock was too hard on him.  In Doris Tock’s opinion,
Justin’s only issue with his father was that he did not stand up to his
mother.   According to Rabbi Sapirman, however, Justin had had problems in the
past with both of his parents.

[
14
]

There was no evidence of any
problem between Goldie and her mother prior to the separation, although Mr.
Tock said that he believes that it upset Goldie when Justin was grounded.

Post-Separation

[
15
]

The parties separated on July 3,
2003 but continued to live under the same roof.  They decided not to tell their
children about the separation until Justin’s and Goldie’s return from summer
camp in August.

[
16
]

There are differing versions as to
how well things were managed during that period.  However, in spite of the
tensions, the parties were able to agree that the three children would remain
in the family home with their mother.  They were hopeful that they would be
able to resolve financial and property issues.

[
17
]

Unfortunately, any chance of an
easy resolution disappeared on September 18, 2003.  Mr. Tock testified that
this was the point at which he realized it was a “pitched battle” between
himself and his wife.

[
18
]

That evening, Mr. Tock and Ms.
Buchbinder Tock argued over a picture that Mr. Tock had taken.  Ms. Buchbinder
Tock claims that Mr. Tock assaulted her; Mr. Tock denies this.  Goldie
witnessed at least part of the altercation.   The other children did not.

[
19
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock called the
police.  After interviewing both parents and Goldie, the police left with Mr.
Tock. While Mr. Tock claims that Goldie saw him leave with the police, Ms.
Buchbinder Tock claims that she did not, as she was already in bed at that
time.

[
20
]

The police took Mr. Tock to the
police station and charged him with assault.  One of the conditions of his bail
was that he not have any contact with his wife.  Mr. Tock went to the home of
his sister, Esther Tock, and did not return to the matrimonial home.

[
21
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock said that in
the days immediately following the incident, the children did not appear to be
upset.  According to her, the atmosphere in the home was more relaxed with Mr.
Tock gone.  Justin was happy when he returned from his school trip.  The family
doctor saw Goldie on September 22, 2003 and reported that she seemed fine.

[
22
]

This was, unfortunately, the calm
before the storm.  When Justin and Goldie returned after an overnight with
their father, Justin yelled and swore at his mother, saying “You’re a terrible
parent.  You lied.  Drop the charges.  Dad said you lied”.  Goldie then started
to cry.  She said, “You ruined my life.  Dad told me he can’t come to my Bat
Mitzvah and it’s your fault”.  Ms. Buchbinder Tock described both children as
“out of control”.

[
23
]

The next day, the children and
their mother went for an appointment at the Jewish Family and Child Service
(“JF&CS”).  During the meeting with the social worker, Justin and Goldie
both yelled, “We don’t like her.  We don’t want to live with her.”

[
24
]

On October 1, 2003, Goldie and
Justin went to have dinner with their father.  He was now living in the house
of his sister, Esther Tock, along with his mother, Doris Tock, his nephew and
his niece.  Goldie and Justin decided that they wanted to live with their
father and did not return home to their mother.

[
25
]

Rabbi Sapirman saw the children
the next day.  He testified that Justin was very angry and that Goldie was
following whatever her brother said.

[
26
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock was quickly
cut out of her older children’s lives.  Two days after the children moved in
with him, Mr. Tock wrote a letter to the vice-principal at Goldie’s school
advising him of Goldie’s change in residence.  He indicated in his letter that
“Goldie has been counselled in measures to take in the event her mother tries
to pick her up against her will”. Without consulting or advising Ms. Buchbinder
Tock, he signed both Justin and Goldie up for camp for the following summer.
Although in the past Goldie had spent one month of her summer at camp and the
other month at home with her mother, Mr. Tock signed her up for two months of
camp.

[
27
]

Doris Tock replaced Ms. Buchbinder
Tock as the primary caregiver for Justin and Goldie.  She drove the children to
school, picked them up, made their meals and ran the household.  She was put
down as the emergency contact on school and camp forms.  Although the children
lived in a one-bedroom apartment in Esther Tock’s house, they had free rein of
the entire house and generally took their meals upstairs with the rest of the
Tock household.  Goldie and Justin were given cell phones so that they could
reach their grandmother if they needed her and so that she could reach them.
Goldie told her mother not to call her on the cell phone because it was for
speaking with her grandmother.  Ms. Buchbinder Tock felt that Goldie and Justin
were no longer her children; they were Doris’.

[
28
]

On one occasion, when Justin came
home to collect his things, he complained to his mother that, while his
grandmother was able to get the children to school and to make their lunches
and dinners, she only got things out of the freezer and put them in the
microwave.

[
29
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock made several
attempts to make arrangements to see her children and to ensure that Goldie and
Justin saw Nili.  While Mr. Tock was interested in him and the three children
getting together, he did not respond positively to his wife’s proposals for
seeing Goldie and Justin.  Mr. Tock’s lawyer suggested that the children could
be reunited if Mr. Tock moved back into the home with all three children and
Ms. Buchbinder Tock moved out.

[
30
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock tried to get
help for the children.  She enrolled them in a program at JF&CS called “One
Family Two Homes” and set up an appointment for them to go for counselling at
the Hincks-Dellcrest Centre.  However, Mr. Tock did not respond positively to
these proposals and Goldie and Justin did not go.

[
31
]

In November 2003, on the motion of
Ms. Buchbinder Tock, the court appointed Dr. Sol Goldstein to conduct a custody
and access assessment.

[
32
]

Mr. Tock reported that Goldie
was very sad in the first few weeks after separation and cried a lot.  Goldie
suffered from stomachaches and was frequently late for school.  Goldie told her
maternal grandmother that the first twelve years of her life had been
miserable.

[
33
]

Goldie’s usual extracurricular
activities were significantly reduced. Her teacher told Ms. Buchbinder Tock
that he had noticed a change in Goldie.  She was uncooperative and was having
difficulty working with her peers.  Another one of Goldie’s teachers reported
that Goldie had verbally threatened her.  This incident was inconsistent with
Goldie’s previous behaviour.

[
34
]

After the move to his father’s,
Justin had an argument with his mother about taking his computer, stereo,
television and other equipment to his new residence.  With the assistance of
his grandmother, Justin hired a lawyer to retrieve his possessions.  The lawyer
contacted Dr. Goldstein and they agreed that this issue be handled by Dr.
Goldstein.  Instead, on a day that he was supposed to see Dr. Goldstein, Justin
removed the goods himself.  He did so with the assistance of his cousin and his
grandmother.

[
35
]

The night before his birthday in
January 2004, Justin called his mother and said that he and his sister would
not come to see her again unless she let Nili come every other weekend.  He
left her a message: “You’ve heard our demands and unless you meet them, you
don’t see us.”

[
36
]

Doris Tock testified that, after
Justin moved in with his father, she helped to bring him out of his shell.  She
reported to Dr. Goldstein that Justin had previously been depressed and never
laughed but that he was now a joy to be around.  She said that he and his
cousin, David, were like brothers.

Dr. Goldstein’s First Report,
February 9, 2004

[
37
]

Dr. Goldstein has been a
psychiatrist for 40 years.  He has conducted an estimated 500 custody and
access assessments since 1968.

[
38
]

In order to conduct his
assessment, Dr. Goldstein met with the parents, the children, Doris Tock,
Esther Tock, David Tock and the children’s maternal grandparents.  He spoke to
the children’s schoolteachers and to Dr. Susan Bradley, a psychiatrist who had
previously seen the parents.

[
39
]

Dr. Goldstein referred to two “Ill
Advised and Unfortunate Incidents”.  The first incident was the charge of
assault against Mr. Tock.  The second incident was Justin’s retrieval of his
possessions.

[
40
]

The purported reason that Goldie
turned against her mother was the charge against her father. Goldie told Dr.
Goldstein that her mother had lied to the police when she said that her father
had assaulted her (the mother) and that it was her mother’s fault that he was
arrested.

[
41
]

Dr. Goldstein noted that Goldie
had witnessed her father being handcuffed and arrested.  While the parties
disagree as to whether Goldie saw her father being escorted out of the house by
the police, they agree that Mr. Tock was not handcuffed.  Dr. Goldstein raised
the possibility of false memory syndrome; that is, that someone had suggested
to Goldie that the handcuffing had occurred and that she had incorporated it
into her memory although it had never happened.   However, while the evidence
is clear that Justin (who was not a witness to the incident) reported to Dr.
Goldstein that his father had been handcuffed, it is not clear whether Goldie
also told Dr. Goldstein that this had occurred.

[
42
]

Goldie was also angry with her
mother because she believed that her mother was keeping her father from seeing
Nili.  She said that her father cried every time that she brought home pictures
that Nili had drawn for him and that it was because “[her] mother will not let
him see [her] little sister”.

[
43
]

The second incident was Justin’s
retrieval of the equipment from his home. Dr. Goldstein was of the opinion that
Justin was out of control.  Justin felt entitled to remove his possessions, to
choose not to be involved in the assessment process and to threaten his
mother.  His father’s family had empowered him to say and do whatever he
wished.  Dr. Goldstein questioned the example set by those who assisted Justin
in removing his belongings.  In his opinion, this assistance both demonstrated
a lack of respect for Justin’s mother and undercut the assessment process.

[
44
]

Justin told Dr. Goldstein that he
had had problems with his mother for a while but that he had always gotten
along with his father.  When asked to describe his problems with his mother, he
said that he did not know what his mother did all day; she did not get anything
done around the house and she talked on the phone all day.  Dr. Goldstein
testified that adolescent boys do not typically make complaints of this kind.
He felt that Justin was repeating what he had heard from the adults around
him.

[
45
]

Dr. Goldstein expressed concern
about Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s difficulty in choosing battles with her children.
However, he had greater concerns about the situation at Mr. Tock’s house.  It
was his impression that “the older children are being rapidly alienated from
their mother and her family”.  With the consent and support of Mr. Tock, Doris
Tock had taken over care of the children and there was no longer any place in
their lives for their mother.  In Dr. Goldstein’s opinion, the children were
embroiled in a struggle between their grandmother/father and their mother.

[
46
]

Dr. Goldstein described the
environment in the Tock household as “toxic” and felt that the situation needed
to be changed urgently. He likened the situation of the children to “prisoners
of war” in that their identities had been taken away from them and their minds
were being worked on.  He called it “the ultimate in child abuse”.   Dr.
Goldstein acknowledged in his testimony that his terminology was extreme but
explained that this was because he felt that the situation was extreme.

[
47
]

Dr. Goldstein recommended that the
parents and children participate in therapy, after which the mother should have
primary care of the three children and the father should have frequent access.
In the meantime, he recommended that the three children have the opportunity to
visit with each other, as well as with their father, at a mutually acceptable
spot other than the father’s residence.  He also raised the possibility that
Goldie and Justin be placed into care while the adults received help.

February 2004 – October 2004

[
48
]

Dr. Goldstein’s report was
released at the end of February 2004.  In spite of the sense of urgency in the
report, the recommendations were not implemented.

[
49
]

Mr. Tock strongly disagreed with
Dr. Goldstein’s conclusions and with the characterization of his family and his
family’s impact on the children.  He felt that Dr. Goldstein was being
apocalyptic and that his recommendations, in some cases, were outlandish.

[
50
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock testified that
when she read the report she was horrified at what the children were going
through and with Dr. Goldstein’s prognosis.  In light of his comments, she was
concerned about Nili going over to the Tock household.  Visits were arranged
for the three children and their father at a Rabbi’s house.  However, Mr. Tock
found those visits uncomfortable and did not feel that the restrictions were
necessary.

[
51
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock testified that
during this period, her relationship with Justin was getting worse.  He told
her not to call or e-mail him.

[
52
]

A disagreement arose between the
parents concerning where, and with whom, the three children would spend the two
Passover seders.  No agreement was reached and, as a result, Nili was with her
mother for the two seders and Justin and Goldie were with their father.   Mr.
Tock sent his wife an e-mail in which he wrote:

“Even I did not think you would
sink to such a low as to purposely and with malice bring harm to your
children.  Enjoy your Sedar’s (
sic
) Evelyn.  Try to find the time in the
next few days to contact your Justin and Goldie and explain to them why you
would refuse to allow them to see their sister… You are sad, Evelyn.  And worst
of all, your children now are seeing just how sad you have become.  We all pity
you.  We will all say a special prayer tonite (
sic
) to G-D for your
return to stable mental health.  Read the Hagadah [the prayer book for the
Seder] closely Evelyn, and as you spill your wine to recall the affliction of
the Jews, spill three more drops for the affliction you have brought to your
own children”.

[
53
]

Another
flashpoint for the parties was Goldie’s Bat Mitzvah plans.  Prior to their
separation, the parties had arranged for Goldie’s Bat Mitzvah to take place on
a boat in June 2004.  Mr. Tock changed the time and place of the Bat Mitzvah
without consulting with his wife.  The effect of these changes was that Ms.
Buchbinder Tock’s family would not be able to have a party with Goldie to celebrate
the occasion, but Mr. Tock’s family would.  A court order was required to
settle the matter.

[
54
]

There was also a court order that
the children were to spend alternate weekends with each parent.  Ms. Buchbinder
Tock was hopeful that the court order for alternate weekend visits would be an
opportunity to reestablish her relationship with Justin.  While Goldie came for
alternate weekends, Justin only came for the occasional Friday night dinner.

[
55
]

The court also ordered that the
children were not to see their grandmothers when they were together on
weekends.  However, the three children did in fact see their paternal
grandmother, Doris Tock, on every weekend when they were together save two.

[
56
]

In June 2004, the court ordered
that Justin and Goldie attend counselling.  Goldie’s counselling started the
following November.  Justin did not go to counselling.

[
57
]

As part of the court-ordered
summer holiday schedule, Ms. Buchbinder Tock was planning to go to Vancouver
with Nili and Goldie at the end of August for a family wedding.  The day before
the planned trip, Mr. Tock advised Ms. Buchbinder Tock by e-mail that Goldie
was away, could not be reached and would not be going to Vancouver.  This
cancellation was precipitated by Goldie’s complaint to JF&CS that her mother
had assaulted her (Ms. Buchbinder Tock denies that the assault occurred).  The
JF&CS followed up and decided not to proceed with the complaint although
they did meet with Goldie for counselling.  This was a serious allegation for
Goldie to have made.  There was, however, no evidence before the court to
suggest that Goldie was or is in any danger of assault from her mother.

[
58
]

After the summer, Ms. Buchbinder
Tock tried to reestablish a schedule for seeing the children.  However, neither
Justin nor Goldie saw their mother between August and November 2004.  Mr. Tock
was frequently away on business trips during this period. In his absence, Doris
or Esther Tock looked after the children.

[
59
]

There were also disagreements
concerning the children’s schools. In September 2004, Nili started grade one at
the Montessori Jewish Day School.  Mr. Tock felt that it was wrong for Ms.
Buchbinder Tock to have enrolled her in the school without discussing it with
him since, prior to separation, they had agreed that Nili would go to a
different school in grade one.  He brought a motion to have Nili removed from
the school but the judge ordered that she remain there.

[
60
]

At the same time, Justin
transferred from Crescent School to Northview, the school his cousin David was
attending.  This transfer was done without consulting with Ms. Buchbinder
Tock.  Ms. Buchbinder Tock felt that Justin should have remained at Crescent;
he had done very well there and it was an academically challenging school.

[
61
]

On cross-examination, Mr. Tock
acknowledged that, while he felt it was acceptable for him to change Justin’s
school without consulting with Ms. Buchbinder Tock, it was not appropriate for
Ms. Buchbinder Tock to change Nili’s school without consulting with him.

Dr. Goldstein’s Second
Report, October 18, 2004

[
62
]

Dr. Goldstein was asked to prepare
an update of his February 2004 report in anticipation of a trial date in
November 2004 (the trial was subsequently adjourned).  He met with both parents
and the three children.

[
63
]

Dr. Goldstein found that the
animosity between the parents had not lessened since he prepared his first
report nine months earlier.  Both were struggling for control of the children
and becoming fixed in their positions.  He was concerned that the situation was
becoming chronic.

[
64
]

In Dr. Goldstein’s opinion, Justin
and Goldie were “running rampant over those around them”.  In their eyes, their
mother could do no right.  Justin and Goldie expressed hatred towards their
mother and Justin felt that he was entitled to openly taunt her.  In Dr.
Goldstein’s presence, he told his mother that he hated her and that he wished
she were dead.   Goldie refused to speak with Dr. Goldstein and her mother
without Justin in the room.  She had no memory of good times with her mother.
Dr. Goldstein was concerned that Goldie was distorting her reality to please
those around her.  For the first time, she exhibited rapid leg movement, a sign
of high anxiety.

[
65
]

Dr. Goldstein recommended that
Goldie be with her mother and that a decision be made as to whether Justin
should be placed with another family or remain with his father. He also
recommended that therapy be instituted as soon as possible and that the
therapist determine the appropriateness of any visits between the children and
Doris Tock.

[
66
]

He noted that:

One cannot expect any changes to the
positive to occur until such therapy begins and until some respect for the
process of returning these children to a more normal way of life where they can
learn to respect one another and society in general as compared to a way where
one manipulates people around in order to obtain what they wish to accomplish.

[
67
]

After Dr. Goldstein completed his
report, he met with Mr. Tock and his girlfriend, Amy Smilestone, at Mr. Tock’s
request.  Mr. Tock and Ms. Smilestone proposed that they set up a home with
Justin and Goldie, away from Doris Tock.  Ms. Smilestone would work towards
reestablishing proper relations with the children’s mother.

[
68
]

Dr. Goldstein was of the view that
Ms. Smilestone might be a person who could help to stabilize the situation.
However, he had several concerns, in particular, whether Ms. Smilestone would
have empathy for Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s situation or would, instead, become a
“cheerleader in the camp of Mr. Tock”.  He concluded that, at this point, the recommendations
in his second report remained the same.  However, he recommended that Ms.
Smilestone and Ms. Buchbinder Tock meet with a mediator and that the situation
be reassessed in six months.  (This mediation did not occur.)

October 2004 – October 2005

[
69
]

Once again, Dr. Goldstein’s
recommendations were not implemented, with the exception that Goldie began
therapy in November.

[
70
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock testified that
she was more concerned about her children after reading Dr. Goldstein’s second
report than after reading the first one.  It was more than a year since Goldie
and Justin had left.  She felt that they were growing further and further away
from her, and that they were still not getting the counselling that they
needed.

[
71
]

Goldie resumed her alternating
weekend visits with her mother in November 2004 having not seen her since
August of that year.  At the same time, she started therapy with her mother at
the Willow Centre.

[
72
]

At some point between January and
March 2005, as a result of discussions during counselling at the Willow Centre,
Goldie’s visits to her mother were increased to include mid-week visits in
addition to the alternating weekends.  Ms. Buchbinder Tock found that progress
in her relationship with Goldie was slow.  Mr. Tock testified that he supported
Goldie’s increased time with her mother.

[
73
]

In April 2005, Mr. Tock, Goldie,
Justin, Mr. Tock’s niece and Ms. Smilestone moved into an apartment in a house
purchased by Mr. Tock’s sister, Esther Tock. It was two doors down from
Esther’s own house.

[
74
]

On May 3, 2005, Justice Backhouse
ordered that Goldie live with each parent on a “week about” basis, that is, on
alternating weeks with each parent.  Ms. Buchbinder Tock wanted Goldie to start
living with her on a full-time basis in September 2005.  Mr. Tock, on the other
hand, felt that the implementation of more time with Ms. Buchbinder Tock should
depend on Goldie’s wishes in conjunction with her counselling  Justice
Backhouse notes in her endorsement “It is not in Goldie’s best interests to
have the pressure of deciding the custodial arrangement given the issue of
parental alienation.  The Willow Centre is acting in a counselling capacity,
not as assessors.”  She further provided that the “week about” schedule was to
be reviewed at the end of August or early September 2005 to see if full-time
with the mother could be implemented.

[
75
]

Although Goldie had told her
counsellor that she did not want the week-about schedule, she started to go to
her mother’s regularly immediately after the order.  At some point, Goldie
began to confide in her mother and to seek her out when she needed her.  Ms.

[
76
]

Over the summer and fall, there
were problems with Nili being returned on a timely basis after her weekend

[
77

Justice Backhouse saw the parties
again on September 14, 2005.  Her endorsement states “Effective immediately,

October 27, 2005

Mr. Tock did not agree that Goldie
should be in Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s primary care.  Dr. Goldstein therefore

79

situation between the parents remained unchanged.  They continued to be

]

The good news is that there was a
major change for the better with respect to Goldie.  Dr. Goldstein found her to

81
]

Unfortunately, for the first time,
there was a visible concern with respect to Nili.  She was very uncomfortable

82
]

Notwithstanding the dilemmas
inherent in any solution, Dr. Goldstein recommended that the recommendations in

[
83
]

He concluded his report with a
cautionary note: “the prognosis for these children’s future, in my opinion, is

84

Ms. Buchbinder Tock has
significant concerns about the impact of Mr. Tock’s mother, Doris Tock, on her

there is no evidence of concerns with respect to them being with their maternal

]

Mr. Tock disagrees that his mother
has had a negative impact on the children.  He presented his mother as a warm

]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock said that she
had never had a good relationship with her mother-in-law.  She claimed that

]

she had accepted her daughter-in-law and would have done anything for her, she

In spite of these strong feelings
about her daughter-in-law, Doris Tock insisted that she had never spoken ill of

89
]

appear to have any insight into the effect of what she was saying on others.
In Dr. Goldstein’s opinion, this was not so much a struggle between father and

the role of mother to the children and there was no room for their real mother
in their lives.

Justin

]

]

this improvement.  The first is the counselling that she, both individually and

]

Notwithstanding this evident
progress, Ms. Buchbinder Tock is concerned that Goldie is on the brink and that

Nili

while last year was a difficult one for Nili, there has been a marked

]

Assessment of the Evidence

[
98
]

This case is as much about
perceptions as it is about credibility.  Each of the parties is committed to
his or her respective version of events.  In assessing the evidence, it
necessary to determine the objective impact of those events on the children.
Mr. Tock may well believe it when he says that he and his family were not
responsible for the rupture of the relationship between the children and their
mother.  They may well not have intended that this happen.  However, it is not
the beliefs nor the intentions of Mr. Tock and his family that are relevant to
assessing the best interests of the children, but the effect of their words and
actions on those children.

[
99
]

The turning point in Goldie’s and
Justin’s relationship with their mother happened at the end of September 2003
and appears to have stemmed from the altercation on September 18th.  It is
uncontradicted that neither Goldie nor Justin was very upset in the days
immediately following the incident.  They only began to blame their mother for
what had happened after a visit with their father, when they said that their
father had told them that their mother had lied and that it was her fault that
he would not be able to go to Goldie’s Bat Mitzvah.  Given this sequence of
events, it is more likely than not that Goldie and Justin blamed their mother
for what occurred not because of what Goldie saw, but because of what their
father had told them.

[
100
]

The children’s history of
their lives prior to separation appears to have undergone substantial
revision.  It is difficult to believe that Goldie and Justin came to their
revised views of their past on their own.  There is no evidence that Goldie was
unhappy or that she had any problems in her relationship with her mother prior
to separation, and yet she said that the first 12 years of her life were
miserable.

[
101
]

According to the testimony
of Doris and Esther Tock, Justin is still angry at his mother for the way in
which she treated him.  While there is evidence that Justin had a hard time
with his parents, this difficult period was more than one year prior to the
separation and more than three years prior to the trial.  The evidence is also
that Justin had problems with both his parents.  However, he now blames his
mother for everything that happened; his father is blameless.

[
102
]

Doris Tock denies that she
ever spoke ill of her daughter-in-law in the children’s presence.   There is no
doubt that she had very strong feelings about her daughter-in-law.  She had no
difficulty in communicating these feelings to Dr. Goldstein and to the court.
Various witnesses described her as a strong and opinionated woman.  The
complaints that Justin made to Dr. Goldstein about his mother echo his
grandmother’s complaints.  It is not credible that Goldie and Justin were
unaware of their grandmother’s feelings concerning their mother.

[
103
]

A review of everything that
was said and done by Mr. Tock in this period points to the conclusion that he
became so involved in the “pitched battle”, which he says began on September
18, 2003, that he was unable to differentiate between winning the battle and
what was in his children’s best interests.  As a result, they too became
embroiled in the struggle.  Instead of Dr. Goldstein’s reports and
recommendations presenting an opportunity to move forward, they became one more
step in Mr. Tock’s battle with his wife.  He acted belligerently towards Dr.
Goldstein, Dr. Collins at the Willow Centre and even Rabbi Sapirman when he
felt that they were not on his side.

[
104
]

Although Mr. Tock and his
sister and mother testified that they tried to encourage the children to repair
their relationship with their mother, the evidence indicates otherwise.  Within
days of Goldie and Justin moving in with Mr. Tock, he counselled Goldie on what
to do in the event that her mother tried to take her away from school, he
registered the children for camp and he made Doris Tock their primary
caregiver.  While Mr. Tock did make attempts in the early days to see Nili and
to reunite the three children, there is no evidence of any efforts on his part
to have the children see their mother.  On the contrary, their mother’s
proposals were rebuffed.

[
105
]

There is no evidence that
Ms. Buchbinder Tock tried to deny Mr. Tock access to Nili although she did try
to impose conditions on that access in order to limit Nili’s exposure to Doris
Tock.

[
106
]

Mr. Tock’s Passover e-mail
to his wife was not only cruel but, more tragically, its language (“We all pity
you.  We will all say a special prayer tonite (sic) to G-D for your return to
stable mental health”) strongly suggests that he involved the children in his
battle with their mother.

[
107
]

Mr. Tock repeatedly said
during the trial that he was just trying to settle things down, to take
gasoline off the fire.  However, his actions say otherwise.  While he excused
his most extreme email, the Passover e-mail, as being unfortunate, it was not
the only email that was problematic.  While he blamed Dr. Goldstein and his
wife for his children not receiving counselling sooner, Ms. Buchbinder Tock
tried to get help for her children shortly after they moved away.  She had to
bring a motion to get an order that they receive counselling.  It was only
after the court order in June 2004 that Mr. Tock took any action,
notwithstanding that Dr. Goldstein’s February 2004 report identified the urgent
need for therapy.

[
108
]

Finally, I turn to the
reports and testimony of Dr. Goldstein.  Mr. Tock contends that Dr. Goldstein
was biased in favour of his wife and against his family.  Dr. Goldstein
testified that, to the extent that he has a bias, it is in favour of the
children and against those children being abused.

[
109
]

Dr. Goldstein did, indeed,
meet with Ms. Buchbinder Tock many more times than he met with Mr. Tock.
However, Ms. Buchbinder Tock requested those meetings.  Dr. Goldstein stated
that had Mr. Tock wanted to meet with him more often, he could have.  When Mr.
Tock did meet with Dr. Goldstein, he often insulted him, telling him that he
was unprofessional and useless.

[
110
]

Mr. Tock also submitted that
Dr. Goldstein did not pursue various avenues that he should have; there were
individuals that he did not interview and stories that he did not corroborate.
However, as Dr. Goldstein explained in his testimony, he was not playing the
role of a detective.  Rather, his job was to try to understand what was
happening with the children and the adults in their lives.

[
111
]

Mr. Tock referred to the
cases of
S.H. v. V. B.
,

[2004] N.B.J. No. 317
(N.B. Q.B. (Fam.
Div.)) and
Gallagher v. Gallagher
,

[1999] N.B.J. No. 324
(N.B.
Q.B. (Fam. Div.)) as echoing the situation here.  In both those cases, the
court stated that the conclusions in the assessors’ reports were not supported
by the evidence.

[
112
]

I do not agree that Dr.
Goldstein’s conclusions were unsupported by the evidence or that he was
biased.  The evidence, both as reflected in his reports and in other evidence
presented during the trial, amply supports his conclusions that Goldie and
Justin were being alienated from their mother.  The fact that Dr. Goldstein
used strong language in both his reports and his testimony is not, in my
opinion, indicative of bias, but reflects the high level of concern that he had
with what was happening to the children.

[
113
]

In the result, I find that
the words and actions of Mr. Tock and his mother, Doris Tock, resulted in the
alienation of Justin and Goldie from their mother.  The Tocks may not have
intended this result, but I find that this is, nonetheless, what occurred.

The Children’s Wishes

[
114
]

The children did not
testify.  However, Goldie’s and Justin’s wishes were made known to the court.
One of the underlying themes of Mr. Tock’s case was that Goldie and Justin very
much wanted to be heard.

[
115
]

It is clear from his actions
that Justin wants to continue to live with his father.  He has resisted being
told what to do by court orders.  The parties agree that ordering Justin to do
anything will have little effect.

[
116
]

The more difficult issue is
Goldie’s wishes and the weight to be given to them.  Goldie has just turned 14
years of age.  She told both Dr. Goldstein and her therapist at the Willow
Centre that she would like things to stay as they are, that is, alternating
staying with each of her parents on a “week about” basis.

[
117
]

However, Dr. Goldstein
expressed the opinion that if children are involved in a difficult struggle
between parents, they should not be put in the position of being asked what
they want.  He felt very strongly that Goldie should be freed of having to make
such a decision.  He explained to Goldie that when she expresses her wishes,
she likely feels that she is displaying favouritism towards one parent or the
other.  He told her that it was for that reason that it was up to him to make a
recommendation and up to the judge to make a decision.

[
118
]

Dr. Goldstein saw Goldie one
more time after having this conversation with her and saw a totally changed
child; she was light and animated.  He felt that one reason for the change
might have been that she was relieved of having to make the custody decision.

[
119
]

Mr. Tock is of the view that
Goldie’s wishes should be respected.  Doris Tock said that Goldie and Justin
should “absolutely not” be ordered to live with their mother but that they
should have the right to decide by themselves.  Esther Tock testified that
Goldie told her that she won’t live with her mother full time.

[
120
]

A child’s wishes,
particularly those voiced by an older child, are an important factor in a
custody decision.  However, those wishes may not coincide with the child’s best
interests.  Listening to a child does not necessarily mean agreeing with her.
As was noted by Weiler J.A. in the Ontario Court of Appeal decision of
Kaplanis
v. Kaplanis
(2005),
2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA)
, 10 R.F.L. (6th) 373 at para.
13
, “While the child’s
best interests are not necessarily synonymous with the child’s wishes, the
older the child, the more an order as to custody requires the co-operation of
the child and consideration of the child’s wishes”.

[
121
]

There are other factors in
addition to the child’s age that may be taken into consideration in determining
the weight to be given to a child’s wishes.  Of particular relevance to this
case is whether one parent may have influenced the child’s decision and whether
one parent has tried to undermine the child’s relationship with the other
parent.  In
Boukema v. Boukema
(1997),
1997 CanLII 12247 (ON CTGD)
, 31 R.F.L. (4th) 329 (Ont. Gen.
Div) at para.
63
, E. Macdonald J. placed less weight on the child’s wishes than
she otherwise would have because those wishes had been greatly influenced by the
mother.

[
122
]

In a case such as this,
Goldie’s wishes must be weighed in the context of the events of the last two
years.  Goldie has been embroiled in her parents’ struggle and has been
alienated from her mother.  There was considerable evidence that Goldie is
easily influenced.  Rabbi Sapirman stated that Goldie “will blow with the
wind”.  His opinion was that she was heavily influenced by her brother and by
whichever side of the family seemed to be stronger.  Esther Tock described
Goldie as wanting to be “everything to everybody”; she tries to please a lot of
people.  As someone who wants to please the people around her, it would make
sense for Goldie to say that she wants to spend equal time with both parents.
She should not be put in the position of having to make that decision.

[
123
]

While I have considered
Goldie’s wishes, I have placed less weight on those wishes than might otherwise
be the case for a 14 year old, given my finding that alienation has occurred
and the evidence that Goldie is someone who is easily influenced.

Compliance with Court Orders
and Undertakings

[
124
]

Each party accuses the other
of having not complied with court orders.  While both parties did not strictly
comply with some orders and undertakings, the most significant breaches had to
do with the children.

[
125
]

There was a complete lack
of compliance by Mr. Tock and his family with the order that none of the
children were to be with their grandmother when they were all together on the
weekends.  Although Mr. Tock maintains that Ms. Buchbinder Tock also breached
the order since Nili has been with her maternal grandmother, the evidence does
not establish that those visits occurred when the three children were together
on weekends.  However, the evidence is that Mr. Tock never kept Goldie and
Justin away from his mother when Nili was over and that any attempt to keep
Nili away from her fell apart after a couple of weekends.  While the order was
admittedly difficult to enforce while the children were living in the same
house as Doris Tock, it was made all the more unworkable by virtue of the fact
that no limits were placed on Justin and Goldie being with their grandmother
when Nili was visiting.  In addition to the fact that the children have been
around their grandmother contrary to the court order, Nili appears to have been
taught not to talk about it.

[
126
]

This breach is very
serious.  It is not just a technical breach but one that goes to the best
interests of the children.  Regardless of whether Mr. Tock agreed with the
order, he was bound to comply with it.  If Mr. Tock felt that the order was
unworkable, he should have brought a motion to vary it.  He did not.  The order
has been in effect since April 2004 and has never been varied or vacated.

[
127
]

There has also not been
compliance with the orders concerning Justin. In spite of the court ordering
that he spend alternate weekends with his mother, Justin did not do so.  He
also did not attend counselling although ordered to do so by the court.  He did
not attend some meetings with Dr. Goldstein and, aided by his cousin and
paternal grandmother, used one of the scheduled appointment times to remove his
possessions. Justin has been taught that he can do as he pleases, even in the
face of a court order.

Relief Sought

(i)
Primary Residence of the
Children

[
128
]

The parties agree that
Nili’s primary residence should continue to be with her mother and Justin’s
primary residence should continue to be with his father.  While one can only
hope that Justin and his mother will be able to repair their relationship, no
court order can make that happen.

[
129
]

The issue in dispute and,
indeed, the key issue throughout the trial, is where Goldie should reside.
While Mr. Tock agrees that Goldie should eventually reside primarily with her
mother, it is his opinion that this should be accomplished through counselling
and should only happen when Goldie wants it to happen.   Thus, what we are
dealing with is the timing of Goldie’s move to her mother’s and whether it
should be court-imposed.

[
130
]

Everyone agrees that Goldie
is doing much better since the “week about” schedule was implemented last May.
Goldie has said that her preference is to continue that schedule.  However, as
noted above, I have placed less weight on Goldie’s wishes than might otherwise
be the case given the alienation that has occurred and the evidence that Goldie
is easily influenced.

[
131
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock feels
that Goldie should reside with her immediately.  While Goldie has improved, she
is concerned that Goldie is at a vulnerable stage.  If she continues to live
with her father half time, Ms. Buchbinder Tock fears that the parental
alienation will continue.  While she acknowledges that there has been progress,
it seems to her that when there is one step forward, there is often also one
step back.

[
132
]

Dr. Goldstein testified
that Goldie’s therapist, Carol-Jane Parker, told him that, in her opinion, the
situation between Goldie and her mother should be allowed to develop.  Ms.
Parker felt that, over time, Goldie would say that she wanted to see her mother
more frequently.

[
133
]

Ms. Parker was not a witness
at the trial.  Mr. Tock wanted to call her to testify as to Goldie’s wishes.
Ms. Buchbinder Tock objected on the basis that Ms. Parker’s testimony would
breach Goldie’s relationship with her therapist and would therefore be harmful
to Goldie.  It was Dr. Goldstein’s opinion that having Ms. Parker as a witness
would be harmful to the therapeutic relationship.  Since there was already
evidence of Goldie’s wishes, I ruled that Ms. Parker could not testify on the
basis that the potential for harm overrode the benefit of the evidence.

[
134
]

Dr. Goldstein disagrees with
Ms. Parker’s opinion.  He is strongly of the opinion that Goldie would be
better off in the care of her mother and that this should be accomplished
immediately through a court order.  He is concerned that absent such an order
there is a significant risk that Goldie will continue to be involved in the
struggle between her parents.

[
135
]

Counsel referred me to
several cases that deal with the issue of parental alienation.  In
Tremblay
v. Tremblay
(1987),
1987 CanLII 147 (AB QB)
, 10 R.F.L. (3d) 166 (Alta. Q.B.), Justice Trussler set
out the overriding principle at para. 9:

I start with the premise that a parent has the right
to see his or her children and is only to be deprived of that right if he or
she has abused or neglected the children.  Likewise, and more important, a
child has a right to the love, care and guidance of a parent.  To be denied
that right by the other parent without sufficient justification, such as abuse
or neglect, is, in itself, a form of child abuse.

[
136
]

Justice Trussler’s
characterization of parental alienation as child abuse echoes the opinion of
Dr. Goldstein when he described the situation at hand.  Justice Trussler stated
at paragraph 16 that, in cases where both parents could equally well look after
their children, it was in the children’s best interests to live with the parent
who was prepared to be co-operative with respect to access.  The evidence here
indicates that Ms. Buchbinder Tock has always been prepared to co-operate with
respect to Mr. Tock’s access to the children, although she has concerns about
their contact with their grandmother.

[
137
]

Reeves v. Reeves,
[2001]
O.J. No. 308 (Sup. Ct.)
is a case with remarkable similarity to the case at
hand.
Reeves
involved two children, aged 16 and 13.  Like Mr. Tock, the
father said that he could not force his children to do anything that they did
not want to do.  He also portrayed himself to the children as the victim in his
marital dispute and presented their mother as the villain.  There were existing
court orders but the children did not believe they needed to comply with them
because their father did not support the orders and did not require them to
follow them.  The social worker who had been appointed by the Office of the
Children’s Lawyer expressed the opinion that, while the father loved his
children and wanted what was best for them, he had a limited ability to
differentiate between his needs and the children’s needs.  In my opinion, these
circumstances mirror the case before me.  Justice Mossip ordered that the
children in
Reeves
be returned to their mother in spite of the fact that
they were 13 and 16 years of age and in spite of the fact that she was aware
that the order would likely cause immediate pain.

[
138
]

While Goldie’s situation has
improved, I saw little evidence during the trial, other than an agreement on
the upcoming holidays, that the battle is over or that Mr. Tock understands the
impact of his actions and those of his family on his children’s well-being.
His lack of insight raises the very real risk that there will be a continuation
of the parental alienation that has occurred in the past.  There is also a risk
that Goldie will continue to be caught in the struggle between her parents.  I
agree with Dr. Goldstein’s conclusion that Ms. Buchbinder Tock is better able
to put aside the battle in order to act in her children’s best interests.

[
139
]

While Mr. Tock says that he
agrees that Goldie should eventually return to live with her mother on a
full-time basis, the evidence suggests that a court order may well be necessary
to accomplish this.  Last winter was the only time that Goldie’s time with her
mother increased without a court order.  On all other occasions, including last
May, a court order was required in order for Goldie to spend more time with her
mother.  While Goldie initially indicated that she did not want the “week
about” schedule, she complied with it once it was ordered and it is now the
regime that she says she wants.

[
140
]

It is in Goldie’s best
interests that, to the greatest extent possible, issues involving her care be
resolved now and by way of court order.  To leave open the issue of where
Goldie will eventually reside and when a change in her primary residence will
happen, raises the very real risk that this issue will continue to be the
subject of a battle between the parties.  This lack of finality would only act
to Goldie’s detriment.

[
141
]

I therefore conclude that it
is in Goldie’s best interests that her primary residence be with her mother and
that this change be effected immediately.  I am aware that the change may not
be easy.  Dr. Goldstein acknowledged that there may be a storm if Goldie is
ordered to move to her mother’s full-time.  However, he was of the opinion that
the ongoing therapy that Goldie and her mother are undergoing should help to
ease the transition.

[
142
]

Mr. Tock’s response to the
situation is critical.  Goldie loves her father and wants to please him.
During his testimony, Dr. Goldstein told Mr. Tock that “if you [her father]
look her in the eye and tell her she should do it, she will.”

(ii)
Co-Parenting or Sole
Custody?

[
143
]

It is Mr. Tock’s position
that, in spite of the events of the last two years, he and Ms. Buchbinder Tock
are capable of putting aside their differences and are able to co-parent.  He
believes that once the trial is over and this decision is rendered, things will
calm down.  He points to the fact that, prior to separation, he and his wife
were able to co-parent in spite of their marital difficulties and that, during the
course of the trial, they were able to arrive at an agreement regarding the
upcoming holidays.

[
144
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock,
however, believes that she and Mr. Tock are not able to co-parent.  At the
beginning of the trial, Ms. Buchbinder Tock sought joint custody of Justin.
However, by the end of the trial, she reluctantly concluded that it was not
workable.

[
145
]

Dr. Goldstein gave his
opinion that Ms. Buchbinder Tock should not be cut out of decisions concerning
Justin and therefore should have joint custody of him.  He recommended that
when the parents could not agree with respect to issues involving Justin, they
could go to an arbitrator.  However, he recommended that Ms. Buchbinder Tock
have the final say with respect to Goldie and Nili because she was better able
to put the children’s interests first.  On further questioning, he suggested
that it perhaps made sense for Mr. Tock to have custody of Justin and Ms.
Buchbinder Tock to have custody of the two girls.

[
146
]

While I would like to
believe that things will calm down after I render this decision, the events of
the last two years do not lead me to conclude that these two individuals are
able to co-parent.  They have called the police on several occasions and have
had frequent recourse to court for matters including: Nili’s school, the
details of Goldie’s Bat Mitzvah service and celebrations, summer holidays in
2004 and 2005, counselling for the children, the celebration of Passover in
2005, Nili’s increased time with her father, Goldie’s increased time with her
mother, and contact with Doris Tock.  Their attempts at dealing with various
parenting issues in the last two years have had a detrimental impact on the
children and, in particular, on Goldie’s and Justin’s relationships with their
mother.  While the parties were able to co-parent prior to separation, the
evidence unfortunately points to the conclusion that they have been unable to
do so post-separation.

[
147
]

As noted by Weiler J.A. in
Kaplanis
v. Kaplanis
(2005),
2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA)
, 10 R.F.L. (6th) 373 (Ont. C.A.) at para.
11
:

“hoping that communication between the parties will
improve once the litigation is over does not provide a sufficient basis for the
making of an order of joint custody.  There must be some evidence before the
court that, despite their differences, the parents are able to communicate
effectively with one another”.

[
148
]

Unfortunately, the evidence
does not support a finding that these parents, post-separation, are able to
communicate with one another in a constructive fashion.

[
149
]

One option would be to order
joint custody and provide that, when the parents were unable to agree, they
would seek arbitration.  Assuming that I have the jurisdiction to make such an
order, I decline to do so.  Given the parties’ history of frequent recourse to
the courts, I am concerned that this option could well be used frequently and
could further harm the children by extending the battle between their parents.

[
150
]

In my opinion, the best
interests of these children demand that opportunities for disagreements between
their parents on parenting issues be minimized.  Unfortunately, the evidence
points to the likelihood that an order for co-parenting would lead to more
opportunities for conflict, not fewer.

[
151
]

It is therefore ordered that
Mr. Tock have custody of Justin and that Ms. Buchbinder Tock have custody of
Nili and Goldie.  Each parent is to provide the other parent with all
information pertaining to the child or children in his or her custody on
matters regarding that child’s health, education and welfare, immediately upon
receiving that information. Each parent has a right to make inquiries and to be
given information as to the health, education and welfare of the child.

(iii)

Contact with Doris Tock

[
152
]

Another issue of contention
between the parties is the extent to which Goldie and Nili see their grandmother,
Doris Tock.

[
153
]

It is Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s
position that Goldie and Nili should not be exposed to Doris Tock except during
the celebration of major Jewish holidays and large family events such as
weddings and Bar and Bat Mitzvahs.  Dr. Goldstein expressed the opinion that it
would be acceptable for the children to be with their grandmother if their
father was also present, but only if he was strong enough to withstand his
mother.

[
154
]

Not surprisingly, Mr. Tock
feels that his mother is not a negative influence on the children and that
their access to her should not be restricted.  He does, however, agree to a
limitation that, for a period of time, the children can only see their paternal
grandmother if either himself or Ms. Smilestone is present.

[
155
]

The evidence indicates that
Doris Tock bears some of the responsibility for the alienation of the children
from their mother.  It is of great concern that the court order that the
children not see their grandmother was so blatantly breached. However, the risk
of Doris Tock having a negative impact on Goldie and on her relationship with
her mother will be significantly reduced once Goldie is residing with her
mother on a full-time basis.  The situation has already improved since Mr.
Tock’s move to another home, albeit a home that is two doors away.  A further
safety net is the therapy that both Goldie and her mother are undergoing.
Finally, Mr. Tock has agreed to an order that he undertake counselling.  That
too should be of assistance.

[
156
]

It is to be hoped that, at
some point, there will be a semblance of normalcy in the children’s lives.
Restricting or prohibiting the children from seeing their grandmother who lives
two doors away from their father is not a normal situation.  If Goldie and Nili
are prevented from seeing their grandmother, there is a risk that this will
provide another reason for Goldie to resist the move to her mother’s.

[
157
]

While I understand Ms.
Buchbinder Tock’s concerns, my opinion is that, on balance, the children’s
access to their grandmother should not be restricted as broadly as Ms.
Buchbinder Tock proposes.  The transition period will be critical for Goldie.
Opportunities for influencing Goldie against the move must be minimized.  I
therefore order that, for a period of six months after Goldie has moved to her
mother’s on a full-time basis, Goldie and Nili only be with Doris Tock when Mr.
Tock is present.  This restriction includes visits to Esther Tock’s home when
Doris Tock is present.

(iv)
Counselling

[
158
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock requests
an order that Mr. Tock undertake counselling for not less than two years, with
a counsellor to be approved by Dr. Goldstein. She further proposes that Dr.
Goldstein be directed to speak with the counsellor for the purposes of
identifying Mr. Tock’s issues and recommending therapy.  Mr. Tock agrees that
he should attend counselling, but proposes that he attend counselling at the
Willow Center under the direction of Dr. Rex Collins for a period of time to be
advised and monitored by Dr. Collins.  He submits that there should be no
information passed from Dr. Goldstein to his counsellor and that any required
updates should be supplied directly to the court, as necessary.

[
159
]

Courts have shown some
reluctance to order that a party undertake counselling.  In
Kaplanis v. Kaplanis

(2005),
2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA)
, 10 R.F.L. (6th) 373 at para.
14
, the Ontario Court of Appeal noted
the problematic nature of such orders.  In this case, Mr. Tock has, to his
credit, agreed to an order for counselling.  In order for that counselling to
be successful, Mr. Tock needs to trust his counsellor.  Mr. Tock has shown that
he would likely not trust a counsellor approved by Dr. Goldstein.  I therefore
decline to order that the choice of counsellor be approved by Dr. Goldstein.

[
160
]

However, I question whether
Dr. Collins is the most appropriate choice of counsellor since he and the
Willow Centre specialize in the treatment of infants, children and
adolescents.  An alternative solution would be that Dr. Collins approve the
choice of counsellor, whether that counsellor be Dr. Collins himself or someone
else approved by Dr. Collins.  Given the difficulties in directing the
counselling process through a court order, I decline to order what
communication, if any, should occur between Mr. Tock’s counsellor and Dr.
Goldstein.  However, I direct Dr. Goldstein to give Mr. Tock’s counsellor
information should the counsellor request it and should Mr. Tock consent to its
release.

[
161
]

Mr. Tock proposes that there
should also be an order that Ms. Buchbinder Tock attend counselling with regard
to aggressive parenting.  She does not consent to such an order.  It is my
opinion that Ms. Buchbinder Tock does not require an order to attend
counselling.  She has always shown a willingness, in fact, an eagerness to
participate in counselling and parenting programs.  The JF&CS reported that
she has been participating in counselling programs with that agency since
September 2003 and that she has agreed to participate in ongoing group therapy
in addition to individual counselling sessions.  She has been actively involved
in counselling with Goldie at the Willow Centre for the past year.

(v)
Nili’s and Goldie’s
Visits with their Father

[
162
]

The parties agree that Mr.
Tock should continue to see Nili on alternate weekends.  However, Mr. Tock
would like to see more of Nili.  He proposes that mid-week visits should start
immediately and take place every fourth Wednesday.  Over time, those visits
would be increased to every other Wednesday.  He proposes that the visits take
place between 5:30 p.m. and 7:15 p.m.

[
163
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock is not
opposed in principle to mid-week access but is concerned that a settling-down
period is required before implementing a new regime for Nili.  She proposes
that the summer time would be a good time to start the new schedule and therefore
that mid-week visits should commence at the end of the school year in June
2006.  She is agreeable to the visits taking place from 5:30 to 7:15.

[
164
]

It is, in my opinion,
reasonable to start the mid-week visits at the end of the school year, to occur
every other Wednesday.  Mr. Tock would pick up Nili at 5:30 and return her by
7:15.

[
165
]

Mr. Tock also proposes that
the regular Sunday drop-off time be extended from 6:00 p.m., the current time,
to 6:30 p.m. and that Nili be able to stay overnight one Sunday a month.  Ms.
Buchbinder Tock had difficulties with Nili’s return time when it was 7:30 since
it did not give Nili enough time to settle down.  Nili is getting older, and it
is my opinion that an extension of the drop-off time to 6:30 is something that
could be managed.  However, given Nili’s age, it is not, in my opinion, in her
best interests to stay overnight on a school night.

[
166
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock
submitted that Goldie should also have alternate weekend visits with her
father.  Those visits should, in my opinion, coincide with Nili’s visits.

[
167
]

Little was said by the
parties about Goldie’s mid-week visits with her father.  There was no reason
put forward as to why those visits could not commence immediately.  Given
Goldie’s age, those visits could also extend later in the evening than Nili’s,
subject to Mr. Tock’s ability to drop off the two children at different times
once the visits with Nili commence at the end of June.  Therefore, Goldie’s
mid-week visits with her father will take place between 5:30 and 9:00 p.m.
every Wednesday.  While Mr. Tock may prefer a more flexible mid-week schedule
for his visits with Goldie, it is desirable to maintain a consistent schedule
for the time being given the conflict between the parents.  That way, both
Goldie and her father will have clear expectations about when they will see
each other and they will not need to involve Ms. Buchbinder Tock in negotiating
their time together.

(vi)

Holiday Schedules

[
168
]

For the same reason that I
am of the view that co-parenting would not work, I am also of the opinion that
a fixed schedule for holidays is required.  Flexibility carries with it the
risk of conflict and, as noted, opportunities for conflict must be minimized.

[
169
]

Mr. Tock and Ms. Buchbinder
Tock have each provided proposed holiday schedules. The only significant
difference between their proposals concerns the choice of holiday weeks during
Christmas and the summer.  Mr. Tock indicated that, as a result of only
recently having joined his current employer, he does not have priority when it
comes to choosing his holiday weeks.  He therefore proposes that, for as long
as he is the only parent who is employed, he should get the first choice of
holiday weeks with his children and Ms. Buchbinder Tock should have the other
weeks.  Ms. Buchbinder Tock, however, is concerned that she will not receive
sufficient notice in order to make holiday plans.

[
170
]

I believe that both
interests can be accommodated by providing that Mr. Tock may have his choice of
week while he is the only one employed so long as he gives sufficient notice of
his choice.  That notice must be given in writing by September 15th for the
Christmas holidays and by April 15th for the summer holidays.  If both parents
are employed or if Mr. Tock does not give the required notice, the weeks will
be alternated as set out in the schedule.

[
171
]

Other than the choice of
holiday week, the two proposals differ only with respect to minor details,
principally the hours at which a parent’s time begins and ends with the
children during particular holidays.  There was no evidence before me that one
time would be better or worse than the other.  I have selected times in order
to ensure a fixed schedule.  The holiday schedule is set out at the end of my
decision.

B.  Property Issues

Net Family Property

[
172
]

During the course of the
trial, the parties advised me as to which property issues were in dispute and
which ones they had agreed upon.  In closing argument, they put forward
different positions with respect to some items.  In my opinion, absent a
further agreement between them, they should be bound by the agreement they put
forward during the trial since the evidence was presented on that basis.  To
allow a party to change his or her position at the stage of closing argument
would be prejudicial to the other party who would not have presented evidence
on the agreed-upon items.

[
173
]

The following items were not
agreed upon:

Car Lease

[
174
]

Mr. Tock claims that, at
separation, there was a debt owing of $7,984.26 on his car lease.  The lease
was for a term of four years from October 2001 to October 2005.  One of its
terms was that Mr. Tock pay for excess mileage. Had the car been turned in on
the date of separation, which was approximately half-way through the lease, the
parties would have owed $7,984.26 on the basis of excess mileage.  However, the
car was not turned in on that date.  Instead, Mr. Tock returned the car at the
end of the lease.  By that time, the amount owing was $2,865.88
.

[
175
]

Mr. Tock submits that the
figure that should be used for the purposes of calculating the equalization
payment is the debt that existed at the date of separation.  He maintains that
the fact that he was able to reduce the loss post-separation is not relevant to
calculating the debt at the date of separation.

[
176
]

Alternatively, Mr. Tock
claims that the amount of debt is the difference between the buy-out price at
separation ($27,471.45) and what the car could be sold for at that time.  He
presented evidence from Auto Trader demonstrating the listing prices of similar
cars around the time of separation. However, this is insufficient evidence of
the value of the car at the time of separation.

[
177
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock
maintains that she should, at most, have to pay her share of one-half of the
final debt, that is, the amount that was due when the car was turned in.  The
debt at that time was $2,865.88.  The parties separated at the approximate
half-point in the lease and she therefore submits that she should be
responsible for her share (one-half) of one-half of the final amount due.
Alternatively, she argues that she should not have to pay anything since Mr.
Tock was reimbursed for mileage by his employer but never declared the
reimbursement as income.

[
178
]

Courts, in general, have
been reluctant to conduct hindsight valuations unless there were facts that
were within the contemplation of the spouses at the time of separation that
would suggest an alternative valuation.   In
Best v. Best
,
1999 CanLII 700 (SCC)
, [1999] 2
S.C.R. 868, the Supreme Court of Canada held that post-separation evidence
could not be used to determine the likely retirement date for purposes of
pension valuation.

[
179
]

In my opinion, it is not
appropriate in these circumstances to conduct a hindsight valuation.  There was
no evidence that the parties had agreed to reduce the debt owing on the car by,
for example, reducing the use of the car.  I therefore conclude that the debt
of $7,984.26 should be included as a debt in the determination of net family
property.

Loan to Larry Buchbinder

[
180
]

Mr. Tock claims that there
was a debt owing from Larry Buchbinder, Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s brother, in the

[
181
]

Mr. Tock has not established
the existence of this debt on a balance of probabilities.

Investment Account

[
182
]

Mr. Tock claims that, on
separation, his wife had an investment account containing $7,500 that Justin
had received for his Bar Mitzvah.  He submits that it should be transferred to
his sister, Esther Tock, for the benefit of Justin.

[
183
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock
testified that she does not have an investment account in this amount and does
not know what Mr. Tock is referring to.

[
184
]

The evidence does not
establish that this account exists.  If Justin does, indeed, still have Bar
Mitzvah money in an account somewhere, it is hoped that the parties will be
able to sort this out.  That account, if it exists, should be made available
for Justin’s benefit.

Children’s Bonds

[
185
]

Mr. Tock proposes that all
bonds and certificates that are in the names of the children be maintained for
their use and not be used by the parents.  Although Ms. Buchbinder Tock is not

Jewellery, Art etc.

[

agreement as to the value of this category of property but, in closing

Legal fees

]

Refund of Boat Deposit

]

]

]

]

Conclusion - Net Family
Property

components of the net family property.  Having made these determinations, the

Other Claims

Occupation Rent

]

Retroactive Housing Costs

[
210
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock submits
that Mr. Tock owes her for costs related to carrying the home from April 1,

[
211
]

Tock was ordered to pay the housing costs until there was a further court

]

]

that it is inequitable that Mr. Tock should benefit from the increase in the
