[
214
]

An added factor in this case
is that Ms. Buchbinder Tock tried to obtain an interest-only mortgage that
would have resulted in significantly lower mortgage costs.  However, Mr. Tock
did not give his consent.  The parties then entered into an agreement whereby
the mortgage was to be replaced by a line of credit.  That agreement was not
implemented because Mr. Tock wanted to add a further amount to the line of
credit to cover certain debts.  As a result, Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s mortgage
payments continued at the rate of $463 per week.

[
215
]

While Ms. Buchbinder Tock
has covered the housing costs since March 2005, she has also had the benefit of
living in the house and has not paid occupation rent.  At the time that she was
ordered to assume the housing costs, she was also granted a significant
increase in spousal support.

[
216
]

In balancing these factors,
it is my opinion that Mr. Tock should not be responsible for the housing costs.

Cost Orders

[
217
]

Mr. Tock agrees that he owes
$3,250 in outstanding cost orders.  What is in dispute is the $500 that the
parties, through their counsel, agreed that Mr. Tock would pay as costs thrown
away in order to avoid a motion.  Ms. Buchbinder Tock had brought a motion to
dispense with Mr. Tock’s consent in the renewal of the mortgage on the home.
In order to resolve the motion, the parties agreed that they would apply for a
personal line of credit in place of the renewal of the mortgage. They also
agreed that Mr. Tock would pay $500 in costs.

[
218
]

However, after the parties’
agreement, Mr. Tock asked to increase the line of credit by $20,000 in order to
cover his credit card debts.  Ms. Buchbinder Tock did not agree to this change
and the agreement was not executed.

[
219
]

Mr. Tock takes the position
that he should not have to pay the costs because the agreement was not
implemented.  I am satisfied on the basis of the evidence that the parties had
a binding agreement and that had Mr. Tock not requested the additional $20,000,
Ms. Buchbinder Tock would have acted on that agreement.  It is therefore due to
Mr. Tock’s actions that the agreement was not implemented.  It is inequitable
for Mr. Tock to now ask the court to relieve him of the costs that he had
agreed to pay.

[
220
]

Therefore, the amount of
costs that accrued prior to this trial and that Mr. Tock currently owes is
$3,750.

C.  Support

Background

[
221
]

There are retroactive claims
for spousal support, child support and sharing of expenses, as well as claims
for ongoing child and spousal support.

[
222
]

In August 2003, the parties
agreed that Mr. Tock would pay $500 per week on a without prejudice basis to
cover household expenses.  After Goldie and Justin moved in with Mr. Tock, he
decreased that amount without obtaining agreement from Ms Buchbinder Tock.  On
February 5, 2004, the court ordered that Mr. Tock pay child support for Nili in
the table amount of $980 per month, based on an annual income of $131,000, and
interim spousal support in the amount of $1,000 per month.  Mr. Tock was also
ordered to pay all expenses related to the matrimonial home.

[
223
]

In January 2005, Mr. Tock
began a job that resulted in a lower income.  He therefore applied for a change
in his support payments.  On March 17, 2005, the court ordered that Mr. Tock
pay child support in the table amount of $706, based on an annual income of $90,000.
Spousal support was increased to $2500 per month and Ms. Buchbinder Tock was
made responsible for the carrying costs of the home until sale.  The order was
made without prejudice to the position of either party regarding the
appropriate quantum of support and who should finally be responsible for the
costs of the home.

Child Support

[
224
]

The following issues need to
be determined:  how to treat Mr. Tock’s bonus for purposes of determining his
income; whether to impute income to Ms. Buchbinder Tock;  whether retroactive
child and spousal support is owing; and camp fees.

Mr. Tock’s Income

[
225
]

Mr. Tock was employed by BBK
until December 2004.  In each of 2003 and 2004, he earned $110,000 in U.S.
currency.

[
226
]

He joined TD Bank on January
17, 2005.  He is a relationship manager in the national accounts section.  His
current base salary is $90,000 plus bonus.  The issue in dispute with respect
to child support is whether Mr. Tock’s bonus should be factored into his income
up front or whether his payments should be based on his base salary, with
adjustments to be made after the bonus has been received.

[
227
]

When Mr. Tock joined the
Bank, he negotiated a bonus of $15,000 for his first year.  However, he
actually earned $104,100

in 2005 since he did not start until mid-January.

[
228
]

Mr. Tock proposes that he be
required to provide his annual bonus information by February 15th and to make a
retroactive payment of any support owing as a result by June 30th, after he has
received his annual tax refund.

[
229
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock disagrees
with this proposal.  She submits that Mr. Tock’s income should be set at
$105,000 ($90,000 base plus $15,000 bonus) and support determined accordingly.
She does not want to have to depend on Mr. Tock to disclose the bonus
information and then to make the retroactive payment.

[
230
]

Mr. Blum, who is also
employed at TD Bank, testified that bonuses are set at some point between
October 31 and mid-December of each year and are paid out in January.  The
amount of the bonus in any particular year depends on a variety of factors,
including individual performance, team performance and bank performance.
According to Mr. Blum, the annual bonus can range anywhere between zero and 15%
of base salary.  While Mr. Tock was able to negotiate a $15,000 bonus in his
first year, there was no evidence as to what it will be in future years, other
than that it is likely to fall somewhere between zero and 15%.

[
231
]

In
Tauber v. Tauber

(2001),
2001 CanLII 28234 (ON SC)
, 18 R.F.L. (5th)

384 (Ont. Sup. Ct.), aff’d (2003),
2003 CanLII 8918 (ON CA)
, 64 O.R.
(3d) 229, Justice Mesbur tackled the issue of how bonuses should be treated.
She explained at para. 44 that child support is prospective and is to be paid
out of current or prospective income.  She stated that “The court is to
determine what the payer will earn, not what the payer has earned.”
Unfortunately, in determining what the payer will earn in the current year, I
am unable to rely on a pattern in the payment of bonuses since Mr. Tock has
only been in his current job for one year.

[
232
]

In
Weismiller v.
Jolkowski
(2000),
2000 CanLII 22518 (ON SC)
, 7 R.F.L. (5th) 453 (Sup. Ct.) Justice Whitten also
addressed the treatment of bonuses and identified the need to balance the
competing hardship to the payor and the needs of those dependent on support
payments.  On the facts of that case, there was a distinct possibility of a
bonus but the amount was unknown.  Justice Whitten advocated using a
conservative approach to determining the quantum of the bonus in order to
minimize the burden to the payor while recognizing the need to pay expenses of
the children year round.

[
233
]

In
T.A.E. v. M.E.E.
(2003),

2003 CanLII 57410 (ON CA)
, 43 R.F.L. (5th) 321, the Ontario Court of Appeal approved of the decision of
the motions judge to average the payor’s bonus over seven years in determining
the amount to be imputed as income for the purposes of paying spousal support.

[
234
]

Unfortunately, there is no
history of bonuses here to enable an averaging approach.  This is not a
situation like
Weismiller
, where there was a trend over the previous
four years that the judge could consider.   Given the absence of a history of bonuses
in this case and the lack of evidence as to what the quantum of the bonus might
be, I am unable to impute an amount of a bonus for the purpose of determining
Mr. Tock’s income.

[
235
]

In these circumstances, an
adjustment will need to be made retroactively once the amount of the bonus is
known.  It is not, in my opinion, reasonable that the adjustment should wait
until June 30, when the amount of the bonus is known by the end of December and
the bonus is received in January.

[
236
]

Mr. Tock should therefore
advise Ms. Buchbinder Tock, in writing, of what his annual bonus is by January
15.  He shall pay on February 1 any amount owing for child support in the
previous year based on the table amount attributable to his salary plus bonus.

Imputing Income to Ms. Buchbinder
Tock

[
237
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock
currently earns no income and has not done so since the parties’ separation.
Mr. Tock takes the position that income should be imputed to her both
retroactively and prospectively.  He did not bring a counter-petition for child
support for Goldie and Justin or for the sharing of expenses, although he did
note these issues in his opening statement and closing argument at trial.

[
238
]

Mr. Tock submits that Ms.
Buchbinder Tock is trained and capable of earning substantial income to help
support the family’s financial needs.  He maintains that his wife’s claim of
fibromyalgia is not proven and that she has provided no evidence that her
physical condition prevents her from earning an income.

[
239
]

Under section 19 of the

Federal Child Support Guidelines
, the court has the authority to impute
income for the purposes of determining child support obligations.  Mr. Tock
claims that the following circumstances exist here: Ms. Buchbinder Tock is
intentionally under-employed or unemployed (section 19(1)(a)); she has failed
to provide income information (section 19(1)(f)); and she has unreasonably
deducted expenses from income (section 19(1)(g)).

[
240
]

The evidence does not
establish that Ms. Buchbinder Tock has failed to provide income information or
has unreasonably deducted expenses from income.  Rather, the evidence
establishes that the income from her two work ventures since separation, that
is, her scrapbooking endeavour and her work as an associate for prepaid legal
services, was less than her expenses.  The issue, then, is whether Ms.
Buchbinder Tock has been or is intentionally under-employed or unemployed.

[
241
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock obtained
a B.A. in physical education in 1985.  After graduation, she took a course in
the travel industry.  From then until the family moved to Peterborough in 1993,
she was employed in various travel agencies, on a part or full-time basis, with
the exception of several months of maternity leave after Justin’s and Goldie’s
births.  Her annual income as a travel agent ranged from $17,000 per year to a
high of $27,500.  She was earning under $20,000 per year at her last job before
the move.  When she moved to Peterborough, she sold her client list to another
travel agency.

[
242
]

After moving to
Peterborough, Ms. Buchbinder Tock looked for work in a travel agency, but was
unsuccessful.  She took a short computer training course and then,
unfortunately, had a serious car accident at the end of 1993.  She was not able
to return to work until the spring of 1994.  She then took a part-time job four
days a week at the Toronto School of Business.  She stopped working just before
Nili’s birth in 1998.  At that point, she had been earning just under $12 an
hour.

[
243
]

After Nili’s birth in August
1998, Ms. Buchbinder Tock did not return to work.  Mr. Tock had lost his job
and they were planning on moving back to Toronto.  She and her husband agreed
that after the move to Toronto, she should stay at home full-time for a period
of time to ease the transition for the children.  The return to Toronto did not
happen until 2000.

[
244
]

At some point after their
return to Toronto, Ms. Buchbinder Tock made inquiries about getting back into
the travel business.  However, the combination of internet bookings and the
post-September 11, 2001 slump in travel made it a bad time to reenter the
industry.

[
245
]

Early in 2003, Ms.
Buchbinder Tock went into the scrapbooking business.  She knew that she would
likely not earn a lot of income from it, but she thought she could earn a bit
of money and get scrapbooking supplies for her own family’s scrapbooks.
Another benefit of the work was that she could do it at night when her husband
was home with the children.  As it turned out, the cost of supplies and other
expenses exceeded any income that she earned.

[
246
]

In 2004, after the separation,
she became an associate for pre-paid legal services.  She earned approximately
$1,200 in total income.  She discovered that the best way to earn money as an
associate was to develop a team.  That work had to be done in the evenings and,
as a single parent, she was unable to do it.

[
247
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock is
currently attending the part-time Early Childhood Montessori Diploma Program at
the Toronto Montessori Institute in order to obtain the necessary
qualifications to become a Montessori teacher.  She decided to take the course
as she was actively involved in Nili’s school and thought that she would be
good at teaching in a Montessori school. Her goal is to finish the course by
January 2007.  She hopes that, upon graduation, she could at least supply-teach
until a regular job becomes available.  The full-time salary for a Montessori
teacher in the first year is $28,000-$32,000.  She does not know how her
physical condition will affect her ability to work but she wants to try and
work at least on a part-time basis.

[
248
]

After Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s
car accident in 1993, she was diagnosed with fibromyalgia.  She still suffers
from joint and tissue pain.  Some days, she has difficulty standing up.  She
has tried various treatments: a chiropractor, acupuncture, massage therapy and
exercise.  In 2004, she began to experience low back pain and was diagnosed
with degenerative disc disease.  She said that she has achieved good results
from exercise, but she still gets flare-ups.

[
249
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s family
doctor, Dr. Sharon Mintz, testified.  She indicated that fibromyalgia is Ms.
Buchbinder Tock’s most significant health issue.  She explained that it is a
constellation of symptoms including chronic pain, fatigue and sleeplessness.
Ms. Buchbinder Tock also suffers from degenerative disc disease and, as a
result, she will always be prone to low back pain which will flare-up with
certain movements.  Dr. Mintz indicated that when she is not experiencing a
flare-up, Ms. Buchbinder Tock should do regular exercise and have good back
control.  Flare-ups are treated by taking anti-inflammatory medication.

[
250
]

I agree with Mr. Tock that
Ms. Buchbinder Tock has not established whether, and the extent to which, her
physical condition prevents her from working.  However, I do not thereby
conclude that she is intentionally under-employed or unemployed.  Mr. Tock and
Ms. Buchbinder Tock had, together, decided that they would move to
Peterborough.  As a result, she left the travel agency business more than a
decade ago. The parties also agreed that on their return to Toronto, Ms.
Buchbinder Tock would stay home for a period of time with the children.  Thus,
her employment situation up to the date of separation was as a result of joint
decisionmaking.

[
251
]

Post-separation, Ms.
Buchbinder Tock has made some attempts at earning an income – through her
scrapbooking business and becoming a prepaid legal services associate – but
neither venture has been successful.

[
252
]

In
Drygala v. Pauli

(2002),
2002 CanLII 41868 (ON CA)
, 61 O.R. (3d) 711, the Ontario Court of Appeal indicated that the burden
is on the recipient spouse to establish what is required by virtue of her
education needs. There are two stages to this inquiry. The first stage is to
determine whether the educational needs are reasonable.  The one area in which
Ms. Buchbinder Tock is trained is the travel industry.  I am satisfied that
reentering this industry is not a realistic alternative.  It is, in my opinion,
reasonable for Ms. Buchbinder Tock to have enrolled in a Montessori teacher’s
course in the hopes of gaining future employment opportunities.

[
253
]

The second stage is to
consider what is required by virtue of those educational needs.  Ms. Buchbinder
Tock’s course is only part-time.  Is part-time employment an option?   Ms.
Buchbinder Tock anticipates that she will finish the course by January 2007.
Given Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s physical difficulties and, most importantly, her
need to ease Goldie’s transition into her home, it is reasonable, in the
circumstances, not to expect her to take on part-time employment at this time
in addition to her course load. Therefore, no income will be imputed to Ms.
Buchbinder Tock.

[
254
]

There is insufficient
evidence, at this point, to make a finding as to whether Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s
physical condition will limit her ability to work on a full-time basis once she
completes her course.

Conclusion – Ongoing Child
Support

[
255
]

In the result, Mr. Tock is
required to pay support for Goldie and Nili in the amount of $1,136, based on
an income of $90,000.  This is to take effect on April 1, 2006, based on an
assumption that Goldie will be residing primarily with her mother within a few
weeks of the release of this judgment.  Mr. Tock is to advise Ms. Buchbinder
Tock of the amount of his annual bonus by January 15.  An adjustment to the
amount of child support paid in the previous year is to be made on February 1
in accordance with the table amount corresponding to his salary plus bonus.

Retroactive Support

[
256
]

In his closing submissions,
Mr. Tock stated that he is seeking retroactive support and a retroactive share
of expenses.  However, he made no prior claim to either and, in any case, no
income has been imputed to Ms. Buchbinder Tock.  His claims are therefore
dismissed.

[
257
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock claims
retroactive support for three periods of time: retroactive child and spousal
support from November 2003 to February 2004, the period prior to the court
order for support and after Mr. Tock decreased his payments; retroactive child
support for the period from January 2005 to April 2005, during which time the support
for Nili was based on an income that did not include Mr. Tock’s bonus; and
retroactive child support from May 2005 to December 2005, the period during
which Goldie was living with her mother half-time.

(a)     November 2003 – January
2004

[
258
]

During this three-month
period, Mr. Tock paid a total of $2,412.53.  No distinction was made between
spousal and child support.

[
259
]

In February 2004, Justice
Greer set the child support at $980 per month, based on an income of $131,000,
and ordered spousal support of $1,000, for a total of $1980 per month.  In my
opinion, this amount of spousal support is a reasonable figure to apply to the
previous three months.  Therefore, Mr. Tock should have paid spousal support of
$1,000 per month and child support of $980 per month for the three months for a
total of $5,940.  The amount owing is $3,527.47.

(b)    January 2005 – April 2005

[
260
]

Mr. Tock’s child support
payments were reduced to $706 based on an income of $90,000 effective April 1,
2005.   However, TD Bank agreed to pay him a bonus of $15,000.   Since he did
not begin at the TD Bank until mid-January, his actual income for the year
(with bonus) was $104,100.

[
261
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock claims
an adjustment in child support for 2005 based on the table amount.  The table
amount for $104,100 for one child is $800 per month.  The change in support
payments was not in effect until April 1, 2005 such that a retroactive
adjustment should be made from that date.  Up to April 1, 2005, the child
support payments were based on a greater income amount.  Therefore, the amount
owing is $94 for the month of April 2005.

(c)   May 2005 – December 2005

[
262
]

There was no increase in
support payments when Goldie began to spend alternate weeks with her mother
after the court order of May 3, 2005.  Ms. Buchbinder Tock claims the table
amount for two children.  Based on an income of $104,100, that amount would be
$1,283 per month.

[
263
]

Section 9 of the
Federal

Child Support Guidelines
provides that, in cases of shared custody,
the amount of child support must be determined by taking into account the
amounts set out in the tables; the increased costs of the shared custody
arrangements; and the conditions, means, needs and other circumstances of each
spouse and of any child for whom support is sought.  In
Contino v. Leonelli-Contino
,

2005 SCC 63 (CanLII)
, [2005] S.C.J. No. 65 (S.C.C.), Justice Bastarache writing for the majority
stated that the wording of that section is imperative, that is, the court must
determine the amount of child support in accordance with the three listed
factors.  He also noted that section 9 requires an emphasis on flexibility and
fairness to ensure that the particular circumstances of each family are
considered.

[
264
]

The situation in this case
is different from that in
Contino
, where it was the payor parent who was
seeking a decrease in support payments based on increased time with his son.
In the case at hand, it is the recipient parent who has increased time with the
child and seeks an increase in the amount of child support.  Notwithstanding
this different fact situation, the general principles set out in
Contino

should
apply.

[
265
]

Turning to section 9(a), the
court is required to consider the amounts set out in the applicable tables for
each of the spouses.  As noted, the table amount for Mr. Tock to pay is $800
for one child and $1,283 for two.  Since I have not imputed any income to Ms.
Buchbinder Tock, there is no table amount that would apply to her.  If one were
to apply the simple set-off approach, that is, calculating the difference
between the table amount of each parent as though each was seeking child
support from the other, then the result would remain a payment of the full
amount of $1,283 by Mr. Tock.

[
266
]

The second factor, set out
in section 9(b), is the increased costs of shared custody arrangements.  Did
Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s costs increase as a result of the increased time that
Goldie was with her?

[
267
]

While in some situations,
the total costs of raising a child in shared custody may be greater than in a
sole custody situation, there is no evidence that this was the situation in
this case.  Prior to the change in Goldie’s arrangements, both parents were set
up so as to be able to house Goldie on a full-time basis.  Ms. Buchbinder Tock
was still in the matrimonial home and Mr. Tock had obtained accommodation that
could also accommodate Goldie on a full-time basis.  Each parent had another
child with him or her, that is, Nili with Ms. Buchbinder Tock and Justin with
Mr. Tock.  Thus, there is no evidence that the fixed costs during this period
varied for either parent.

[
268
]

An examination of the
parties’ financial statements provides some limited assistance.  When I compare
Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s expenses as set out in her financial statements of
November 2004 and November 2005, the one significant change is in the “children”
column, with expenses changing from $185.82 per month in 2004 to $511.50 per
month a year later.  Mr. Tock’s most recent financial statement reflects his
actual budget for 2005 and therefore does not show what difference the change
in Goldie’s arrangements made.  There was no direct evidence on either party’s
part as to how the “week about” arrangement changed their expenses.

[
269
]

The final factor to be
considered is set out in section 9(c): the conditions, means, needs and other
circumstances.  As seen in both parents’ respective financial statements, the
period leading up to trial has been a difficult one financially for both of
them.  Both parents have significant debt-loads.  Both parents had full-time
responsibility for one child while sharing responsibility for Goldie.  Both
parents were also in a period of transition.

[
270
]

While the financial
pressures on both parents are significant, it is Mr. Tock’s pay cheque that has
to cover the cost of all of the children’s needs in addition to spousal
support.  Through factors beyond his control, Mr. Tock experienced a
significant decrease in his income at the beginning of 2005.  He continued to
have full-time responsibility for Justin and received no financial contribution
for his care.  He paid the significant camp fees for Justin and Goldie.

[
271
]

After considering all of the
factors, I conclude that a fair result would be a contribution of $1,000 per
month for the support of Nili and Goldie during the time that the “week about”
schedule was in place.  Mr. Tock paid $706 per month during this period.  In
the result, he owes $294 per month from May 2005 to December 2005.  Child
support should continue at the amount of $1,000 until the end of March 2006,
after which there will be a new amount of child support reflecting the change
in Goldie’s primary residence.

Camp Fees

[
272
]

The parties agree that
extraordinary expenses under section 7 of the
Federal Child Support
Guidelines
are to be agreed to by the parties before expenses are incurred
and will be shared proportionately to their incomes.  However, they disagree as
to how Justin’s and Goldie’s camp fees for 2006 should be treated.  Those fees
amount to $10,500.

[
273
]

Mr. Tock seeks an order that
he be able to retain his annual bonus for 2005 in order to pay Justin’s and
Goldie’s camp fees.  That, in my opinion, would be contrary to the way in which
the
Child Support Guidelines
are structured.  There is an entitlement to
child support in the table amount based on the parent’s income.  Mr. Tock’s
income includes his bonus.

[
274
]

Any additional payments are
to be considered within the purview of section 7 of the
Guidelines
and,
if they qualify under that section, are to be shared by the parties in
proportion to their incomes.

[
275
]

In considering whether the
camp fees qualify as an extraordinary expense, I have to consider “the
reasonableness of the expense in relation to the means of the spouses…and the
family’s spending pattern prior to the separation” (section 7).

[
276
]

While Justin and Goldie went
to camp prior to separation, Goldie only went for one month.  It was Mr. Tock’s
decision to enroll Justin and Goldie in camp for 2006.  He did not consult with
Mr. Buchbinder Tock or obtain her agreement.

[
277
]

In considering the means of
the spouses, I note that Mr. Tock’s income of $90,000 plus bonus is the only
income available to the parties at the current time.  Both parties have
significant expenses and debts.  In these circumstances, it is my opinion that
an expense of $10,500 for summer camp is not reasonable given the means of the
spouses and does not qualify as an allowable expense under section 7.
Therefore, Ms. Buchbinder Tock should not be required to contribute to this
expense.

[
278
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock agrees
to complete any forms required to apply for an abatement of their camp fees.

Spousal Support

[
279
]

The parties agree that Ms.
Buchbinder Tock is entitled to receive spousal support.  At issue is the amount
of support and whether there should be a period within which no variation of
this support may be sought.

Quantum

[
280
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock has been
receiving spousal support in the amount of $2,500 since a court order in March
2005.  She proposes that support continue at that amount.

[
281
]

Section 15.2
of the
Divorce
Act
sets out the applicable factors and objectives for the determination of
spousal support.  The court must take into consideration the condition, means,
needs and other circumstances of each spouse including the length of time the
spouses cohabited; the functions performed by each during cohabitation; and any
order, agreement or arrangement relating to support (
s.15.2(4)
).  The
objectives of a spousal support order are: the recognition of any economic
advantage or disadvantages to the spouses arising from the marriage or
breakdown of the marriage; an apportionment of the financial consequences
arising from the care of a child of the marriage beyond the child support
obligation; relief of any economic hardship of the spouses arising from the
breakdown; and promotion of the economic self-sufficiency of the spouses within
a reasonable period of time and in so far as is practicable (
s. 15.2(6)
).

[
282
]

In
Bracklow v. Bracklow
,

1999 CanLII 715 (SCC)
, [1999] 1 S.C.R. 420, the Supreme Court of Canada undertook a comprehensive
review of spousal support.  McLachlin J. summarized the statutory provisions
and case law at para. 49 and set out three conceptual bases for entitlement:
compensatory; contractual; and non-compensatory.  Although in many cases
entitlement is found on either a compensatory basis or on the basis of a prior
agreement, there may still be a support obligation where a need is established
absent an agreement or an entitlement to compensation.

[
283

While entitlement is not at

entitlement (
Bracklow v. Bracklow
, supra
at para.
50
). No one factor
predominates.  Rather, the court is required to consider a number of factors
and arrive at an amount based on the particular facts of the case.

[

]

This was a 17 year marriage.
The parties have three children.  After this decision, Ms. Buchbinder Tock will
continue to care for Nili, the youngest child, on a full-time basis and Mr.
Tock will continue to care for Justin.  It is Goldie’s living arrangements that
will change: Goldie will cease to be with her parents on a “week about” basis
and will reside primarily with her mother.

[
285
]

Although Ms. Buchbinder Tock
worked at various times in the marriage, she is, in my opinion, economically
disadvantaged as a result of the marriage and as a result of joint decisions
made by her and Mr. Tock.  She left the travel agency business in 1993 when the
family moved to Peterborough and has not been successful in reentering it.  She
was not employed between Nili’s birth in 1998 and the separation in 2003 (other
than during her brief but unsuccessful attempt to earn some income in the
scrapbooking business), again, largely as a result of decisions that both
parties made.   She was the primary caregiver for the three children during
this period.  With respect to her situation since separation, I refer to the
discussion in the section on imputing income for child support purposes.

[
286
]

On the basis of the
compensatory model, it is reasonable that Ms. Buchbinder Tock be supported to
enable her to overcome the economic disadvantage that she has sustained and to
enable her to become self-sufficient.  I am satisfied that obtaining her
credentials to become a Montessori teacher is a reasonable step towards
achieving self-sufficiency.

[
287
]

Mr. Tock feels under
significant financial pressure.  His is the only pay cheque at the current time
supporting two households.  His base salary is $90,000 and in 2005 he earned a
bonus of $15,000.  After this order, he will continue to care for Justin on a
full-time basis.  He will not receive a contribution from Ms. Buchbinder Tock
for Justin’s support for the foreseeable future since she has no income at the
present time.

[
288
]

Mr. Tock lives with his
girlfriend, Ms. Amy Smilestone, who earns $30,000 plus a bonus of an estimated
$5,000.  Ms. Smilestone pays half of the rent and household bills and her
proportionate share of the groceries.  Mr. Tock’s financial statement, dated
November 2005, shows a significant debt-load.  Excluding mortgage payments and
disposition costs, his debts total approximately $113,000.  His largest debts
are tax arrears, credit card debts and a loan from his mother.  He says that he
has no available credit remaining.  Mr. Tock’s financial statement shows a
monthly deficit of $5,139 (after an adjustment is made to accurately reflect
Ms. Smilestone’s contribution to the rent).

[
289
]

While Mr. Tock’s expenses
should decrease somewhat after Goldie moves to her mother’s, his child support
payments will increase.  Mr. Tock’s support payments are currently not deducted
at source due to his tax arrears.  Once those arrears are paid, there should be
some easing of his cash-flow difficulties.

[
290
]

Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s
financial statement of November 2005 shows a comparable debt-load to Mr.
Tock’s.  Excluding mortgage payments and disposition costs, her debts total
approximately $110,000.  Her largest debts are personal loans and legal fees.
Assuming support payments of $3,206 ($706 for child support and $2,500 for
spousal support), her financial statement shows a monthly deficit of $3,400.
Her child support payments will increase as a result of this decision, but her
expenses will increase as well.  Her mortgage payments as of November 2005 were
$1,900 per month.  There was no evidence as to what her mortgage payments will
be after she obtains Mr. Tock’s interest in the matrimonial home.

[
291
]

Neither side has a significant
asset other than their interest in the matrimonial home.  Neither party has an
exorbitant life-style.   Justin and Goldie go to public school.  While Nili
attends a private school, she has obtained a full bursary.  The one significant
discretionary expense given the family’s income is summer camp for Goldie and
Justin (at a cost of approximately $10,500).  Mr. Tock hopes to obtain an
abatement of camp fees.  If he does not, this is a significant sum given the
family’s income.

[
292
]

There are a few financial
unknowns: what Mr. Tock’s annual bonus will be; whether he will receive an
abatement of the children’s camp fees; and what Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s mortgage
payments will be.

[
293
]

The fact that this is a
split custody situation is a factor.  Both parents have the financial
responsibilities that come with children residing with them on a full-time
basis.  Mr. Tock has been paying spousal support in the amount of $2,500 since
March 2005, while Ms. Buchbinder Tock has been paying the mortgage and other
housing costs.  As a result of this judgment and the change in Goldie’s primary
residence, Mr. Tock’s child support payments will increase.  At the same time,
Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s expenses relating to the children will increase.

[
294
]

For the purposes of
determining the family net disposable income, I have not initially added in an
amount for Mr. Tock’s bonus since I am unable to determine an appropriate
amount given the lack of a history of bonuses.  Since Ms. Buchbinder Tock’s
childcare responsibilities are greater than Mr. Tock’s in that she will have
two children with her while he will have one, and since I have not added in an
amount for the bonus into the calculations, it would be reasonable to allocate
to her a proportion of the family net disposable income that is somewhat
greater than half.  At Mr. Tock’s current rate of remuneration, that is
$90,000, the rate of support of $2,000 would give Ms. Buchbinder Tock 53.6% of
the total net disposable income.  Were Mr. Tock to earn a $15,000 bonus this
year as he did last year, a spousal support payment of $2,000 would give Ms.
Buchbinder Tock 50.4% of the total net disposable income.  This amount is, in
my opinion, reasonable given the circumstances.

[

There are two variation

limitation on seeking a variation.

[

Ms. Buchbinder Tock
originally proposed that spousal support be increased annually by the
percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index.  She was, however, agreeable
to Mr. Tock’s proposal that it be increased by the lower of the percentage
increase in the Consumer Price Index and the percentage increase in Mr. Tock’s
income, provided that the income included Mr. Tock’s bonus.  Mr. Tock, however,
submits that the annual increase in income should be based on his base salary
alone.

[
297
]

It is not known at this time
whether there will be a regular pattern of bonuses.  On the other hand, basing
the annual increase on the increase in Mr. Tock’s salary alone is not representative
of the true increase in his income.  In these circumstances, it is my opinion
that the increase to the spousal support payment should be based on the
increase in the Consumer Price Index.

[
298
]

With respect to seeking a
variation, Ms. Buchbinder Tock submits that there should be no adjustment to
spousal support until January 2009 and then, only if there is a material change
in circumstances.  She contends that she will need time after graduating from
her course to find employment and to find out if she has physical
limitations.   She also submits that it would be good for all concerned if the
parties were able to avoid litigation for a while.  It is Mr. Tock’s position
that a 2009 limit on review is unreasonable.

[
299
]

Either party could
experience a material change in financial circumstances.  It is, in my opinion,
inappropriate to limit either party’s ability to seek a variation should there
be a material change.

[
300
]

This is a family in
transition.  Custody and access will change as a result of this order.  Ms.
Buchbinder Tock hopes to finish her course in January 2007.  She will likely
need some time in which to find employment.  She does not know the extent to
which her physical difficulties will limit her ability to work on a full-time
basis.  Mr. Tock has not been with his current employer long enough to have
established a patterns of bonuses.  In these circumstances, it is reasonable to
permit either party to seek a review of spousal support after January 1, 2008
without having to establish a material change in circumstances.

Mr. Tock agrees to maintain
a term life insurance policy with Ms. Buchbinder Tock as the principal

fact that she does not currently have a support obligation.
